nicheStories.title: Surprise strikes signal Iran is digging in for a long war
nicheStories.description: In recent weeks, Iran has gone on the offensive, striking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and launching a surprise attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. From a distance, these moves look like self-defeating escalation. Why should a badly damaged state, under severe economic pressure, lash out at the U.S. instead of pushing for a ceasefire?The answer, simply put, is that Iran is digging in for a long war. Whatever Washington's intentions, Tehran increasingly interprets sanctions, negotiations, temporary ceasefires and military strikes as different instruments aimed at a single objective: regime change. As long as this primary objective remains, Iran expects no sanctions relief or meaningful de-escalation. My conversations with Iranian foreign policy analysts suggest that Tehran now believes the war will continue in different forms until the end of Donald Trump's presidency. There is no doubt that the war has punished Iran’s economy. Over 23,000 U.S. and Israeli strikes heavily damaged the country's energy, industrial, transportation, and civil infrastructure, which had kept the country functioning despite decades of onerous sanctions. The country is experiencing the largest contraction in its labor market, along with the highest inflation rate, in its modern history.Beyond economic costs, the war has profoundly changed Iran’s perception of costs and its decision-making logic. The February 28 decapitation strike did not replace old, conservative political leaders and military commanders with more hard-line ones dominated by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as mainstream U.S. media has suggested. Instead, it formed a shadow decision-making system that is more confident, less patient, less predictable, and guided by a different calculation of risk. Iran's experience of failed negotiations with the U.S. before the two major airstrikes in 2025 and 2026 intensified this new perception. In Tehran's view, a comprehensive agreement with the Trump administration is virtually unachievable. Trump either cannot deliver a durable settlement because he cannot afford its domestic political cost, or he does not want to. Even if the administration wants to change course, Israel, which clearly maintains substantial influence within Trump’s inner circle despite the recent rhetoric of Vice President JD Vance, will do what it can to disrupt it. The debate over the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is illustrative. Under the MoU, bombing stopped, and the blockade was lifted despite some violations of the Lebanon ceasefire. But the promised economic incentives were never realized. Tehran exported $6 billion in oil but did not receive the $12 billion in foreign assets it had expected. This limited implementation of the deal hurt Iran’s negotiating team at home.Sources told me that Iranians were also deeply dissatisfied with the Qatari-administered mechanism for allocating Iran’s frozen assets to import essential foods and medicine, and blamed Doha for misleading them.Altogether, these deepened the suspicion that the United States had paused its attacks in order to rebuild its defenses, update its military targets, bring oil prices down, and manage domestic grievances before returning to war. Ironically, hawks in the U.S. complained that the MoU had allowed the Iranians to rebuild their military capabilities in the interim.In Iran, a fragile MoU with no clear economic benefit was seen as a one-sided pause that exposed the Islamic Republic to societal and political pressures that had eased during wartime. While inflation, unemployment, poverty, and mismanagement fueled public anger, power struggles among political and security factions intensified. On one hand, Tehran could wait, ignoring some of Washington’s violations of the MoU while taking advantage of its limited economic benefits, and retaliating if the U.S. resumed the war. A factor weighing on the minds of leaders was that a renewed full-scale war would target Iran’s remaining energy, industrial, and civilian infrastructure, on which the state still depends. However, the leadership in Tehran came to believe that the relative benefits of waiting flowed overwhelmingly in favor of the United States and Israel. In particular, as long as Washington controlled the tempo of the war and decided when the war began, paused, and resumed, Tehran would lack agency.Seeking to break the deadlock, Tehran has thus adopted a strategy of managed confrontation, a form of active deterrence to raise the cost for the United States. Such a confrontation is limited enough to avoid full-scale war but would still increase political pressure on the Trump administration. Even limited attacks can disrupt the U.S. military’s focus, spread out its forces, engage its defensive systems, and force it to spend more on defensive operations than on preparing for a resumption of the war. At the same time, Tehran could keep negotiation channels open and demonstrate its desire for diplomatic solutions.Iran’s economic experience reinforces a confidence that Iran can win this gamble. Iran has absorbed enormous damage without collapsing. As the government allows inflation and currency depreciation to rise, goods keep moving; shelves are not empty, although fewer people can afford what is on them. Iran’s diverse geography helps to bypass the blockade and meet its essential needs. Its privileged welfare system has protected public employees on whom the effective functioning of the state relies, but much of the burden falls on informal workers and small firms. In contrast, a fragile MoU without economic benefits, combined with high uncertainty, will not ease the war’s economic burdens but will lower the cost of a new U.S. attack. As such, a controlled confrontation is more worthwhile.Iran's military and geographic leverage over the Strait of Hormuz helps the country raise the costs of war in a way that could exhaust Trump, perhaps forcing him to abandon the confrontation and change his Iran policy. The pressure is growing: as public support in the U.S. has declined, Trump’s popular approval has fallen to an unprecedented low. Of course, Tehran may underestimate Trump’s tolerance for a prolonged conflict. Another risk is that, while Tehran might be able to calibrate the targets and scale of its own attacks, it cannot control how Washington responds. In addition, Iran's neighbors may lose patience with Iran’s retaliatory attacks on them and join the U.S. in the attack.Finally, domestic discontent over the destruction wrought by the war (on top of a collapsing economy and increased repression) remains a persistent possibility that would fracture wartime solidarity. Still, Iranian leaders appear determined to continue down a path of extended, low-grade war.For Washington, the upshot of this change in Iranian thinking is straightforward. If the U.S. is truly interested in ending the war rather than engaging in endless military confrontation, it must recognize the limits of military pressure. The military campaign might be effective in damaging Iran’s military and economic infrastructure, but, until now, it has been politically counterproductive. It has heightened Iran’s economic crisis and increased poverty, but failed to force Iran's capitulation. More military strikes are most unlikely to alter this seeming paradox. What may yet change this state of affairs is a U.S. effort to incentivize de-escalation. If even part of the $12 billion promised by the MoU had actually reached Iran, its leadership would have been much less likely to take the military initiative. That is the lesson of the broken memorandum: Washington has put enormous effort into making escalation costly, but far too little into making restraint worthwhile. Until that changes, more pressure is unlikely to end Iran's resistance; instead, it may reinforce the lesson Tehran least wants to hear: that resistance is still the only option that pays.

nicheStories.title: American veterans know the cost of a military-first foreign policy
nicheStories.description:
My nearly 32-year career in uniform has taught me many lessons. One of the most important is that the gap between operational military success and strategic political outcomes can be significant and is rarely, if at all, closed by increased military activity.It is common to invoke military voices when arguing for military force and to treat restraint as a “civilian” position. But the reverse is often true. Those who have served, and seen and felt the impacts of warfare, are the most cautious about resorting to it. Leading with, and relying on, the military has never been a foundational U.S. value. Throughout much of its history, the country has rightly regarded the use of force as a last resort. In his Farewell Address, George Washington warned that "overgrown military establishments" were "inauspicious to liberty." U.S. professional military education teaches Carl von Clausewitz’s theory that military force must remain subordinate to political ends. Colin Powell, as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, argued that military force should only be used to achieve clear, definable objectives supported by public opinion. Other retired military officers, including those cited by Andrew Bacevich and Daniel Sjursen in Paths of Dissent, have offered similar arguments.The imbalance in U.S. statecraftThe U.S. military is taught to think about national power through the DIME or DIMEFIL models: diplomatic, informational, military, economic, financial, intelligence, and law enforcement. In theory, those elements are designed to work together. But, in practice, the post-9/11 wars have left the military far more ready and resourced than its civilian counterparts, which are the elements necessary to shape political outcomes.This imbalance is documented by past and current funding requests and appropriations bills. Recent military budgets are nearly $900 billion a year, with upwards of another $600 billion requested in 2026. By contrast, international affairs budgets (funding diplomacy, development, and security assistance) are closer to $50–60 billion. The disparity is therefore roughly 15-to-1, or upwards of 25-to-1 if indeed a $1.5 trillion defense budget is approved.In “How Everything Became War and the Military Became Everything,” Rosa Brooks bluntly states the challenge: when the military is the only fully resourced instrument of foreign policy, every problem starts to look like it has a military solution. In 2008, two colleagues and I published a complementary argument in American Diplomacy, citing then-Defense Secretary Robert Gates' appeal for "a dramatic increase in spending on the civilian instruments of national security." In the nearly two decades since, the spending gap has only widened, and diplomacy and development funding has been cut to historic lows.Too often, military operations are initiated to “send a message,” and troop deployments are announced without clear political aims or criteria for their withdrawal. This over-reliance on military solutions has become an expensive habit.Where military tools meet political realityAfter an initial decade in the infantry, I spent most of my career working at the civilian-military seam of multiple U.S. agencies and with foreign military forces operating under their own political environments. That experience offers a unique perspective — one the restraint community draws on too rarely.
U.S. law divides foreign military engagement into three distinct categories of assistance, each with their own unique legal and political requirements and associated costs: training and equipping; advising and assisting; and direct employment of U.S. forces. Several observations apply across all three:
First, security cooperation relationships tend to outlast the political rationales that created them. The State Department's 2024 International Security Advisory Board stated the problem concisely: “Security cooperation commitments are easy to initiate but remarkably difficult to draw down, restructure, or terminate responsibly when a partner’s strategic alignment degrades.”
Second, over time, every relationship opens a gap between Washington's intent and what is achieved on the ground. One key analysis in 2017 described it as a principal-agent problem or the “divergence between the outcome the principal seeks and the outcome the principal obtains.” The difference can be reduced only when those managing the relationship frankly acknowledge that its original objectives are no longer being met.
One example of this, according to the Journal of Strategic Studies report, is that despite massive assistance from the U.S. during the Iraq War, the Iraqi Security Forces that emerged from the training mission “proved far less proficient than was hoped.”
Third, military forces operate inside specific political environments that they did not create or fully understand. While training and equipping can improve foreign security force capabilities, these efforts have little influence on civil-military relations, corruption, or other governance challenges. A 2018 comparative study, “Building Militaries in Fragile States,” and the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction both drew the same conclusions from different environments. When civilian instruments of national power are not resourced to support a functioning political environment, the military takes on tasks it is neither designed nor trained to do.
I served in Iraq when the U.S. military, the Iraqi army, and the Kurdish peshmerga built Combined Security Mechanisms along one of Iraq's most dangerous fault lines in 2010, creating a series of checkpoints and shared patrols that kept armed actors who did not trust each other operating toward a common purpose. They were designed as a temporary solution, not a permanent presence, and they helped manage a security seam; they could not resolve the political disputes beneath it. The lesson was not that U.S. forces should have stayed, but rather that when a military operation concludes, fully resourced diplomatic and political entities need to be deployed. By June 2014, the Islamic State was able to exploit that seam as it seized Mosul and drove toward Baghdad.Restraint as strategic discipline Restraint means using U.S. military power in a disciplined, deliberate way to achieve clear objectives grounded in an honest assessment of likely costs and consequences. The foundation of responsible statecraft is that foreign policy should not be organized around the objective of global military dominance. In “A New Foundation for U.S. Grand Strategy,” Barry Posen argues for a strategy focused on protecting core security interests. But restraint is not just theoretical; it must be practically applied. It cannot be achieved when the military is fully funded but the civilian elements of national security are under-resourced.
The civil-military divide is important. The decision to use force belongs to elected civilian leaders, and the military should not get a veto. The military's obligation is to offer its best operational advice, execute lawful orders, and respect constitutional authority. This is a discipline running from former Secretary of State George Marshall's example through Kori Schake's contemporary analysis. 
Veterans don’t have more authority to decide, but they enjoy more political space to speak out. What those who have served add to the discussion is perspective: not of how recent conflicts should have ended sooner, but rather whether the military must keep shouldering the burdens for which other, now severely depleted instruments of national security were originally built.The cost of a military-first policyU.S. wars and conflicts over the past quarter century have resulted in an estimated 30,000 service-member and veteran suicides (more than four times the number killed in operations), and veteran long-term care costs are one of the largest components of military compensation. Defense budgets that outgrow those of their civilian counterparts are not fiscally responsible; the differences result in even greater costs tomorrow. Those costs are largely paid by the post-9/11 military cohort as well as their families and communities.
I have seen firsthand a part of the price we pay through adaptive scuba diving instruction with disabled veterans whose injuries result from policy decisions made years before. A military-dominated foreign policy, without clearly defined political goals and adequately resourced civilian institutions to achieve them, will result in many more veterans needing care for decades to come. 
A country that leans so heavily on its military owes it to those who serve to fund and resource the other elements of national security, so when military force is deployed it is used appropriately and not because the other tools of national security are not ready. Political leaders protect the military service members they deploy by ensuring this balance exists. 
Force can be a precise instrument, but its consequences can be unpredictable. Treating the military as the first tool of statecraft, while the other instruments of national security are under-resourced, will remain costly in both dollars and lives.

nicheStories.title: Bored of Peace: Why is Trump undermining his own Gaza plan?
nicheStories.description: A lot can change in a week. Barely five days after President Donald Trump hailed the “historic agreement” on Hamas’s disarmament by the Board of Peace (BOP) — the body Trump created to oversee his Gaza Peace Plan — the very same Board of Peace has now effectively reneged on its own agreement. The deal emerged from eight months of intensive negotiations between BOP High Representative Nicolay Mladenov and Hamas, along with various regional stakeholders, and was expected to pave the way for implementing the long-delayed second phase of Trump’s 20 Point Plan. This would have included desperately needed reconstruction and the establishment of a Palestinian governing body and police force, alongside the disarmament of Hamas and withdrawal of Israeli forces from the devastated enclave. Trump and his BOP had already given Israel an effective pass on most of its Phase 1 obligations, refusing to call out Israel’s daily violations of the ceasefire. Israel has persisted in carrying out near daily airstrikes across Gaza, killing at least 1,250 Palestinians since the ceasefire was signed last October, even as it continues to severely restrict aid, seize more territory, and block the return of Palestinian governing and policing bodies.Last week’s agreement would’ve required each side, notably Israel, to meet all of its outstanding obligations. The two most contentious points — distinguishing between heavy weaponry and small (private) arms, and the sequencing of weapons decommissioning and Israeli withdrawal — were finally agreed after intense pressure on Hamas by the Egyptians and other interlocutors. Most crucially, the deal called for a parallel, phased process in which Israeli military withdrawal and the decommissioning of Hamas weapons occurred concurrently — a pragmatic provision that would ensure progress and prevent either side from exercising a “veto” over the process. Keen to make the deal work, Trump administration officials even lodged an implicit threat, warning that if Israel rejected the plan, “obviously President Trump would be very, very disappointed.”But Israel rejected the terms of the deal, insisting there would be no Israeli withdrawal unless Hamas was fully disarmed and Israel maintained the freedom to continue conducting military operations in Gaza. Instead of calling Israel out, the Trump-aligned BOP did a complete about-face, adopting the Israeli position wholesale. “Contrary to inaccurate reports,” read Monday’s BOP statement, “we note that the withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators [emphasis added].” Of course, the agreement said no such thing. Article 8 of the BOP’s Road Map expressly states that the decommissioning “process is linked to a phased Israeli withdrawal from the areas it controls in Gaza and the inventorying of weapons held by armed militias.” Indeed, Mladenov himself had said “Withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning.” As such, Trump’s Board of Peace has essentially rewritten its own peace plan, requiring Hamas to meet all of its Phase 2 obligations even before Israel has met any of its Phase 1 obligations.The implications of the Trump administration’s whiplash-inducing turn will be serious and far-reaching. First and foremost, it badly undermines Mladenov’s credibility as a broker. If anything he negotiates can be so quickly and easily negated by the White House, why should Hamas — or for that matter other regional actors like Egypt and Qatar — talk to him? Trump is also undercutting his own peace plan more broadly, jeopardizing one of his few concrete foreign policy achievements. Hamas is unlikely to go along with this latest shifting of the goalposts; after all, the demand that the group unilaterally disarm even as Israel entrenches and expands its control over Gaza while carrying out deadly attacks on a daily basis would be widely (and accurately) viewed as surrender. Most devastatingly, for Gaza’s 2.2 million inhabitants, who have already withstood unspeakable horrors and are now living in the most horrid of conditions, Trump’s U-turn will indefinitely delay desperately needed relief, recovery and reconstruction.
